extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in media effects and media bias
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedia-style overview of the hostile media effect — the tendency for partisans to perceive identical media coverage as biased against their side — including its definitions, empirical studies, cognitive explanations, moderators, mediators, consequences, and suggested remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile media effect (definition / core phenomenon)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hostile media effect is the tendency for individuals with strong opinions on opposite sides of a controversial issue to both perceive identical news coverage as unfairly biased against their own position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement compares perceptions of the same content across partisan groups; key empirical signature is that both opposing partisans view identical content as hostile to themselves. Examples: Vallone, Ross & Lepper (1985) study; Sabra and Shatila filmstrip study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective recall refers to memory and retrieval: partisans tend to remember more of the disconfirming portions of a message than the parts that support their position (a variation of the negativity effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vallone et al. observed selective recall differing along partisan lines even on objective criteria such as the number of references to a given subject. Note: some studies document hostile media even when selective recall is positive rather than negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective perception refers to the process by which individuals perceive what they want to in media messages while ignoring opposing viewpoints; partisans have a heightened tendency to interpret aspects of a message as unfavorable or hostile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing and existing values/beliefs shape interpretation; selective perception is treated as a form of bias because information is interpreted congruently with prior beliefs. Cited as a core cognitive mechanism for HME.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards / motivated reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Also called the different standards explanation or motivated reasoning: partisans apply different standards to arguments, confirming what they already believe and developing rationalizations to dismiss contrary evidence, driven by desire to avoid cognitive dissonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads perceivers to see a small sample of media as unrepresentative of the larger 'population' of evidence they accept, producing charges of bias. Vallone et al. quote illustrates that partisans expect the sampled presentation to be unrepresentative and infer hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source factors (characteristics of message source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of the message source influence HME: a source perceived as friendly to the partisan is less likely to invoke the effect than one perceived as disagreeable or geographically detached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: identical content presented as a newspaper triggered HME more than when presented as a student essay. Perceived similarity of a TV host reduces perceived bias. Source reach and perceived affiliation matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisanship (audience composition and strength)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hostile media effect requires an audience of partisans; stronger devotion to a side correlates with stronger manifestations of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing ideological commitment increases biased information processing; both protective motives (personal values) and group affiliation explanations apply. Nonpartisans show much weaker or no HME.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative hostile media effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When media messages are non-objective, partisans on both sides may recognize bias but the group the message opposes perceives a greater degree of bias than the group the message supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated in studies (e.g., primate testing coverage). Also, individuals sometimes evaluate objectively biased articles as 'even-handed' if bias targets the opposition. Observed variations across ideology (some studies find stronger HME among conservatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderator — Reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Reach of the publication moderates the effect: HME is more likely when participants estimate effects of mass media with large reach; low-reach media often elicit biased assimilation instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gunther & Schmitt argued reach explains divergent responses to ambiguous material; participants faulted ambiguous mass-reach information but supported lower-reach reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderator — Involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue involvement is positively correlated with HME: the more involved or invested individuals are in an issue, the stronger the hostile media perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects found for value-relevant and affective involvement; some studies also find effects among low-involvement individuals, but involvement typically amplifies HME.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderator — Social identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Social identity processes moderate HME: ego-involving coverage activates group identity, increasing salience and prompting ingroup members to derogate media coverage perceived as unfavorable to protect group self-esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outgroup membership of the message source matters: attacks attributed to an outgroup elicit greater perceived bias, while ingroup attributions may reduce perceived bias. Social identity theory explains coping via biased perceptions to restore esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediator — Selective categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective categorization: partisans categorize more content as unfair to their position than as fair, influencing perceived bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed by Perloff as a key mediator; operates alongside selective recall and different standards to produce hostile perceptions rather than mere opinion differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediator — Prior beliefs about media bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior beliefs about media bias: generalized negative beliefs about the media predispose partisans to judge specific content unfairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perloff identifies this as one of four mediating reasons why highly involved individuals perceive hostile bias; prior skepticism toward media amplifies HME.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile media online / digital-age considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: HME in digital media: partisan users can interact with content and attribute effects to social media messages; relative effects may be higher as partisans easily agree posts are biased but oppose side perceives greater hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal and empirical evidence suggests social media news messages (e.g., Facebook) produce hostile perceptions and presumed strong effects on third persons; interactivity and selective exposure complicate remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence — Persuasive press inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasive press inference: individuals infer the direction or slant of news they view, generalize that slant to news overall, assume high-reach news influences public opinion, and thus conclude public opinion opposes their cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research is mixed on real-world translation; perceived hostile media can lead to corrective actions, feelings of disenfranchisement, defiance (including undemocratic actions), or withdrawal from political activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence — Motivated fake news perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivated fake news perception: partisans from opposing sides can perceive the exact same news message as 'fake' to significantly different degrees depending on issue stance and source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tsang and others show partisan motivations shape judgments of fakeness, interacting with perceived source motives and policy support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible remedy — Media literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Media literacy interventions: competency in analyzing and evaluating media messages has been tested as a remedy to HME with limited and mixed results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 2014 study found media literacy PSAs had strong effects in some areas but not others; literacy messages can sometimes spur further selection into agreeable enclaves and may not reduce perceived hostility toward opposing sides. Empathy interventions produced greater perceived favorability toward one's own position but did not reduce perceived hostility toward the opposing side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible remedy — Presentation of sources / context manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing context or the source channel (e.g., presenting identical content as a student essay rather than a newspaper article) can reduce or eliminate HME, though it may produce biased assimilation in other ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gunther & Schmitt's study: HME disappeared when GM food content was presented as a student essay vs newspaper. However, in essay conditions participants judged persuasiveness as favorable to their own side, consistent with biased assimilation — remedy trade-offs exist.
